body.p: The ending shows the person, so the pronoun is left out: **Γράφω** "I write", **Γράφουμε** "we write". **-ουνε** for **-ουν** is common in speech: **Πού μένουνε;** "Where do they live?"

The **dictionary form** is the first person singular, **γράφω**, not an infinitive. Greek has no infinitive like English "to write"; it uses **να** + verb instead (chapter 22): **Θέλω να γράψω** "I want to write".

ex.en: What are you doing? I'm working.
Where do you live? We live in Pangrati.

solved.a: μένω, μένεις, μένει, μένουμε, μένετε, μένουν | μένω, μένεις, μένει, μένουμε, μένετε, μένουνε

check.why: Greek dictionaries list the first person singular.

sections.title: The two stems of every verb

body.p: Every verb has a **present stem** and an **aorist stem**. The aorist stem usually adds **-σ-** or changes the last consonant:

The **aorist stem** is used for the simple past, the simple future (**θα γράψω**), the subjunctive (**να γράψω**) and the imperative (**γράψε**). The **present stem** for the present, the imperfect (**έγραφα**), the continuous future (**θα γράφω**) and the continuous subjunctive (**να γράφω**).

ex.el: Γράφω ένα μήνυμα. / Θα σου γράψω αύριο.
ex.en: I'm writing a message. / I'll write to you tomorrow.

ex.el: Αγοράζω ψωμί κάθε μέρα. / Αγόρασα ψωμί.
ex.en: I buy bread every day. / I bought bread.

ex.el: Ανοίγει στις εννιά. / Μπορείς να ανοίξεις το παράθυρο;
ex.en: It opens at nine. / Can you open the window?

check.q: Θα σου ___ αύριο. (simple future of γράφω)
check.why: The simple future uses the aorist stem.

sections.title: The eight forms in one table

head: Continuous (present stem)
Perfective (aorist stem)
rows: έγραφα I was writing, I used to write
θα γράφω I'll be writing, I'll write (regularly)

body.p: Add the **perfect** tenses, built with **έχω** + the invariable form **γράψει** (chapter 25): **έχω γράψει** "I have written", **είχα γράψει** "I had written", **θα έχω γράψει** "I will have written".

The **past tenses** stress the third-last syllable. When the stem is too short for that, an **augment έ-** is added in front and carries the stress: **έγραφα, έγραψα**. When the word is long enough, there is no augment: **γράψαμε, γράφαμε** (chapter 19).

ex.en: I was writing when the phone rang.
I'll write to you every week.
I'll write to you as soon as I arrive.
I want to write to him.

solved.q: "I was reading when you called." (διαβάζω, παίρνω τηλέφωνο: πήρες)
solved.why: Ongoing past action: imperfect; the interruption: aorist.

solved.q: "I'll call you tomorrow." (παίρνω τηλέφωνο, aorist stem πάρ-)
solved.why: One action in the future: θα + aorist stem.

solved.q: Give the 8 forms of **αγοράζω** in the first person
solved.a: αγοράζω, αγόραζα, αγόρασα, θα αγοράζω, θα αγοράσω, να αγοράζω, να αγοράσω, αγόραζε/αγόρασε
solved.why: Present stem αγοραζ-, aorist stem αγορασ-.

check.q: Χθες ___ ένα ωραίο βιβλίο. (I bought, once)
check.why: A single completed past event: aorist.

check.q: Όταν ήμουν παιδί, ___ πολλά κόμικς. (I used to read)
Αύριο θα ___ στη γιαγιά. (I'll write, once)
check.why: Single future action: θα + aorist stem.

check.q: Από τώρα και στο εξής θα ___ κάθε μέρα. (I'll exercise: γυμνάζομαι)
check.why: Repeated future action: θα + present stem.
να + aorist stem for a single action.
Imperative of a single action: aorist stem.

check.q: "I used to work in a bank." (δουλεύω)
check.why: Imperfect for a past state or habit.
Imperative, aorist stem; second accent before το.

sections.title: Aspect: the key to the Greek verb

body.p: The choice between the two stems is **aspect**: how you **view** the action, not when it happens.

list: **Continuous** (present stem): the action is ongoing, repeated, habitual, or seen from the inside, without its end.
**Perfective** (aorist stem): the action is one complete event, seen as a whole, often with a result.

head: Continuous
Perfective
rows: Έτρωγα όταν ήρθες. I was eating when you came.
Έφαγα και βγήκα. I ate and went out.
Κάθε μέρα θα τρέχω. I'll run every day.
Αύριο θα τρέξω πέντε χιλιόμετρα. Tomorrow I'll run five km.
Πρέπει να διαβάζεις κάθε μέρα. You must study every day.
Πρέπει να διαβάσεις αυτό το βιβλίο. You must read this book.
Μην τρως γλυκά! Don't eat sweets (as a habit)!
Μη φας το γλυκό! Don't eat the cake (that particular one)!

body.p: Words that point to the continuous: **κάθε μέρα, συνήθως, πάντα, συχνά, όλη μέρα, ενώ, την ώρα που**. Words that point to the perfective: **μία φορά, χθες το βράδυ** (for a single event), **αμέσως, μόλις, ξαφνικά**.

solved.q: "Don't drink so much coffee!" (a habit, πίνω)
"Don't drink that coffee, it's cold!" (once, πιω)
solved.a: Μην πιεις αυτόν τον καφέ, είναι κρύος!

solved.q: "While I was cooking, the phone rang." (μαγειρεύω, χτυπάω)

check.q: Μπορείς να μου ___ το αλάτι; (pass: δίνω, once)
Ενώ ___, άρχισε να βρέχει. (we were walking: περπατάω)
Όλο το καλοκαίρι ___ στη θάλασσα. (we swam, again and again)
check.why: Repeated action over a period: imperfect.

check.q: "While I was sleeping, someone called." (κοιμάμαι: κοιμόμουν)

check.answer: Θα σε παίρνω τηλέφωνο κάθε μέρα.

check.q: "Don't eat the cake!" (one specific cake, informal)
check.why: One occasion: μη(ν) + aorist stem φα-.

check.q: "I was reading when the light went out." (διάβαζα, έσβησε)

body.p: Many common verbs exist only in **-ομαι** with an active meaning: **έρχομαι** "I come", **κάθομαι** "I sit", **θυμάμαι** "I remember", **φοβάμαι** "I'm afraid", **χρειάζομαι** "I need" (chapters 26–27).
To use a verb fully you need its **principal parts**: present, aorist, passive aorist and past participle.

ex.el: Πλένω τα πιάτα. / Πλένομαι και φεύγω.
ex.en: I'm washing the dishes. / I'll have a wash and go.

ex.el: Έχασα τα κλειδιά μου. / Χάθηκα στην Πλάκα.
ex.en: I lost my keys. / I got lost in Plaka.

ex.el: Το μαγαζί είναι κλεισμένο; Όχι, κλειστό.
ex.en: Is the shop closed? (shut up) No, closed (for the day).

check.why: Washing yourself: πλένομαι (Πλύθηκα would be "I had a wash", past).

title: How the Greek verb works
part: Μέρος Ε΄ | Το ρήμα | The verb
blurb: Persons and endings, the two stems of every verb (present and aorist), the eight forms built from them, aspect explained with everyday examples, and the principal parts to learn.

intro.p: The Greek verb looks big, but it is built from a small kit: **two stems** and **two sets of endings**. Every verb has a **present stem** (**γράφ-**) for actions seen as ongoing or repeated, and an **aorist stem** (**γράψ-**) for actions seen as single, complete events. Put **θα**, **να** or an augment in front, add the endings, and you have all the tenses.
Learn each new verb with its **aorist**: **γράφω – έγραψα**, **αγοράζω – αγόρασα**, **πίνω – ήπια**. Once you know the two stems, the rest is automatic.
